guides.title: How to Set Up Meld Studio: Your First Stream, Start to Finish
guides.one_liner: Your first stream in Meld Studio, start to finish — scenes, mic, Kick or Twitch, no stream key, no plugins.
guides.description: New to Meld Studio? Set up your first stream step by step — download, scenes, mic, connecting Kick or Twitch, and going live. No stream key, no plugins.
guides.body:
New to streaming, or new to Meld? This is the whole road: download to live, in plain steps. Nothing here needs a plugin, a second program, or a computer science degree. It's only metal — let's bolt it together.

Before you start

You need:

  • A computer (Windows 10/11 or macOS 12+)
  • A camera — a webcam is fine to start
  • A microphone — even the one in your headphones beats no mic
  • Internet with decent upload — wired ethernet if you can, Wi-Fi if you must (more on this in the bitrate guide)

Step 1: Get Meld

  1. Go to meldstudio.co and download Meld Studio. It's free — no watermark, no time limit, no account needed to start.
  2. Install it and open it.

Coming from OBS? Meld can import your existing OBS scenes in one click, so you don't rebuild everything from scratch.

Step 2: Build your first scene

A scene is what your viewers see — your layout. A layer is one thing inside it: your game, your camera, a picture, a webpage.

  1. Click the + next to Scenes to make a new scene.
  2. Right-click the scene and Rename it — call it "Live".
  3. In the Layers panel (left side), click the + icon.
  4. Pick Game Capture for a fullscreen game — it grabs the game automatically. For a window or your whole screen, pick Display Capture instead.
  5. Click + again and pick Video Device, then choose your camera from the dropdown.
  6. Drag the camera layer where you want it. Drag the corners to size it. Layers higher in the list sit on top of layers below them.

Make two more scenes the same way when you're ready: "Starting Soon" and "BRB". Same layers, calmer picture. You don't need them today.

🧰 Field note — from the bench: CleanDEE's go-to scene stack — which scenes he actually uses on stream and which ones turned out to be decoration — drops in here.

Step 3: Add your microphone

  1. Find the Audio Mixer and click the + next to it to add a track.
  2. Choose your microphone as the input.
  3. Talk at your normal stream volume. Watch the meter: you want it bouncing in the green/yellow, not living in the red. Red means distortion — turn the track down or move the mic back a touch.

Want the fan and the keyboard clicks gone? Add the Voice Clarity filter to your mic track: on the track, click the + in the filters rack, pick Voice Clarity, and try the Moderate strength first. (Older Meld versions call this filter Magic Mic — same job.) The full audio walkthrough is in Audio Basics.

Step 4: Connect Kick or Twitch (no stream key needed)

Meld talks to Kick and Twitch directly — no copying stream keys for either one.

  1. Open the Outputs panel (top-right corner of Meld).
  2. Click the + icon.
  3. Pick Kick or Twitch from the list.
  4. Click Login and sign in through the browser window that opens. Your stream key fills itself in.
  5. Turn on Start this stream when going live in that output's settings.

Streaming to both at once? Add both outputs. Meld multistreams built-in — one Go Live sends to every output you've turned on.

Before your first real stream, set your title and category on the platform itself (your Kick or Twitch dashboard). Do it before you hit the button, not after.

Step 5: Set your numbers (keep it simple)

  1. Open Settings → General.
  2. Set Main Canvas to 1920×1080.
  3. In Stream Settings, leave the resolution at 1080p to start.

The settings Meld recommends for Kick, and a good starting point all round:

SettingValue
Resolution1920×1080
Frame rate60 fps
Hardware encoderOn (NVENC if you have an NVIDIA card)
Video bitrateUp to 8,000 kbps (your upload decides — see the bitrate guide)
Audio bitrate160 kbps or higher

If your internet or PC struggles, drop to 720p before you drop anything else. A stable 720p beats a dying 1080p every single time.

Step 6: The pre-flight check

Before you press Go Live, every time:

  • ☐ Camera shows you, framed the way you want
  • ☐ Mic meter moves when you talk, stays quiet when you don't
  • ☐ Game or screen capture shows the right thing
  • ☐ Headphones ON if you're listening to anything (speakers feed your mic and give your viewers an echo)
  • ☐ Title and category set on the platform
  • ☐ Test recording first if anything changed since last stream: record 30 seconds, watch it back

Step 7: Go live

  1. Click Go Live.
  2. Say the thing. Be the human. Everything else is just plumbing.

🧰 Field note — from the bench: CleanDEE's first-stream story and the one mistake he tells every new streamer to skip — coming when he writes it.

Related guides: On OBS instead? How to Set Up OBS Studio for Streaming. Overlay next: How to Add Overlays to Meld Studio and OBS. Picture smearing? Why Is My Stream Blurry?

faq.q: Is Meld Studio free?
faq.a: Yes — a free download with no watermark and no time limit, and you don't need an account to start.

faq.q: Do I need a stream key to stream on Kick or Twitch with Meld?
faq.a: No. Meld talks to both platforms directly: add the output, click Login, and Meld fills the stream key in for you.

faq.q: Can Meld Studio multistream?
faq.a: Yes. Add more than one output — Kick and Twitch, say — and one Go Live sends to all of them. It's built in, no plugins.

faq.q: Can I bring my OBS scenes into Meld?
faq.a: Yes. Meld imports your existing OBS scenes in one click, so you don't rebuild your layout from scratch.

guides.title: How to Set Up OBS Studio for Streaming: Your First Stream, Start to Finish
guides.one_liner: The OBS road in plain steps — install, scenes, mic, stream key, and the exact Kick and Twitch settings.
guides.description: Set up OBS Studio for streaming step by step — install, scenes and sources, mic, stream key, and the exact Kick and Twitch settings — then go live.
guides.body:
OBS is the old workhorse — free, powerful, runs everything. It's also less hand-holdy than Meld, so here's the whole road in plain steps: install to live.

Before you start

  • A computer, a camera (webcam is fine), a microphone
  • Internet with decent upload — wired beats Wi-Fi, every time

Step 1: Get OBS

  1. Go to obsproject.com and download OBS Studio for your system. It's free.
  2. Install and open it. If it offers an auto-config wizard, let it run — it's a decent first guess at your settings.

Tip: right-click your OBS shortcut and try Run as administrator if game capture ever shows you a black screen. Some games only let an admin-level program see them. (Full story in the troubleshooting guide.)

Step 2: Build your first scene

A scene is a layout. A source is one thing inside it.

  1. In the Scenes box (bottom-left), click + and name it "Live".
  2. In the Sources box, click + and add:
    • Game Capture — for a fullscreen game
    • Video Capture Device — your camera
    • Audio Input Capture — your microphone (or set the mic once for every scene in Step 3)
  3. Drag sources in the list to stack them: camera above game, game above background. Higher in the list = on top on screen.
  4. Click a source in the preview to move and resize it.

Later, add "Starting Soon" and "BRB" scenes the same way. Not today.

Step 3: Set your mic once, for every scene

  1. Open Settings → Audio.
  2. Set Mic/Auxiliary Audio to your microphone.
  3. Set Sample Rate to 48 kHz — and set your mic to 48 kHz in your system sound settings too. Mismatched sample rates are the number-one cause of voice slowly drifting out of sync on long streams.

Now the mic exists in every scene. Talk, and watch the Mic/Aux meter in the Audio Mixer bounce in the green/yellow.

Step 4: Connect your platform

Twitch

  1. Settings → Stream → Service: Twitch.
  2. Connect Account and sign in (recommended), or paste your stream key from your Twitch Creator Dashboard → Settings → Stream.

Kick

OBS has no built-in Kick preset — the connection is manual, and that's normal:

  1. On Kick, open your Creator Dashboard → Channel → Stream URL and Key. Copy the server URL and the stream key.
  2. In OBS: Settings → Stream → Service: Custom…
  3. Paste the server URL in Server and the key in Stream Key.
  4. Apply.
  5. Set your stream title and category in the Kick dashboard BEFORE you start — Kick can refuse to start cleanly without them.

The settings Kick demands

Kick is strict. Outside these lines the stream can fail or get rejected:

SettingValue
EncoderH.264 only (x264, NVENC H.264, or AMD HW H.264)
Rate controlCBR (variable bitrate is NOT supported)
Bitrate1,000–8,000 kbps
Keyframe interval2 seconds (in Settings → Output)
Resolution / fpsUp to 1920×1080 at 60
AudioStereo, 48 kHz max

Kick's own rule: your upload speed should be at least twice your bitrate. 6,000 kbps stream = 12 Mbps upload, minimum.

Twitch's published guideline tops out at 6,000 kbps for non-affiliates, so if you multistream to both, 6,000 is your ceiling.

Step 5: The pre-flight check

  • ☐ Camera framed right
  • ☐ Mic meter moves when you talk, quiet when you don't
  • ☐ Game capture shows the game (not a black box)
  • ☐ Headphones on — speakers feed your mic and echo to viewers
  • ☐ Title and category set on the platform
  • ☐ Record 30 seconds and watch it back if anything changed

Step 6: Go live

  1. Click Start Streaming (bottom-right).
  2. That's it. You're a streamer. Stay awesome, humans.

🧰 Field note — from the bench: CleanDEE ran OBS for his FPV and work streams — his honest take on OBS vs Meld for different kinds of streams lands here.

Related guides: Trying the newer app? How to Set Up Meld Studio. Blurry picture? Why Is My Stream Blurry? Something broke? Stream Troubleshooting: The Big Five Fixes.

faq.q: How do I connect OBS to Kick?
faq.a: There's no built-in Kick preset, and that's normal. In your Kick Creator Dashboard open Channel → Stream URL and Key, then in OBS pick Settings → Stream → Service: Custom… and paste the server URL and key in.

faq.q: What bitrate should I use in OBS?
faq.a: Kick allows 1,000–8,000 kbps and wants your upload at least twice your bitrate. Twitch's published guideline tops out at 6,000 kbps — so if you stream to both, 6,000 is your ceiling.

faq.q: Do I need a stream key for OBS?
faq.a: For Twitch you can Connect Account and skip the key entirely, or paste the key from your Creator Dashboard. Kick is always manual: server URL plus key, as above.

faq.q: Why is my game capture black?
faq.a: Most often OBS needs to run as administrator — some games only let an admin-level program see them. The full hunt is in the troubleshooting guide.

guides.title: How to Add Overlays to Meld Studio and OBS
guides.one_liner: One permanent overlay link, pasted in and sized right — plus the audio-track step everybody misses.
guides.description: Add an overlay to your stream in Meld Studio or OBS: paste one link, size it right, and turn on the audio track everyone forgets — plus how to test alerts before you go live.
guides.body:
Your ForeverHumans overlay lives at one permanent link — your link, nobody else's, and it never changes. Your alerts, pop animations and sounds all ride that one link. Set it up once and forget it exists. That's the whole point.

This guide drops that link into Meld first, then OBS.

Get your link

  1. Open your ForeverHumans toolkit dashboard.
  2. Copy your overlay link. (Crew tip jar, link page and panels each have their own links — this one is the overlay.)

Guard this link like a stream key. Anyone holding it can put your alerts on their screen.

In Meld Studio ⭐

  1. Open the scene you want the overlay on (usually your main Live scene).
  2. Copy your overlay link.
  3. Click on the Meld canvas and paste (Ctrl+V / Cmd+V). Done — Meld turns a pasted URL into a Browser layer by itself.

Prefer the long way? Layers panel → + → Browser, then paste the URL into the URL field in the Inspector panel.

  1. Drag the layer to full screen — overlays are built for 1920×1080. Use Lock Size on the layer if you don't want it resizing when you nudge it.

The step everybody misses: overlay SOUND

A Meld browser layer is silent by default. Your alerts will show but never make a noise until you do this:

  1. Select the Browser layer.
  2. In the Inspector, under the URL field, turn on Add an audio track for the source.
  3. Want to hear the alerts yourself? Turn on CUE on that audio track. Your viewers hear it either way — CUE is for YOUR ears.

Overlay looks frozen or stale? Click the reload icon next to the URL field to refresh the layer.

🧰 Field note — from the bench: CleanDEE's overlay placement habits — where he keeps alerts so they never cover the action — goes here.

In OBS Studio (Browser Source)

  1. In the Sources box, click + and pick Browser.
  2. Name it something honest, like "FH Overlay".
  3. Paste your overlay link in the URL field.
  4. Set Width 1920 and Height 1080 for a full-screen overlay. (A standalone alert box usually wants 800 × 600 instead — the toolkit tells you the size on the same screen you copied the link from.)
  5. Tick Refresh browser when scene becomes active — your overlay wakes up fresh every time you switch to that scene.
  6. Click OK. Drag the source to the TOP of the Sources list so alerts draw over your game, not under it.

Test it before it counts

  1. Back in your toolkit dashboard, hit Fire a test (or ask the Roadie: "test my overlay").
  2. You should see the pop animation AND hear the sound.
  3. See it but can't hear it?
    • Meld: you skipped the audio track step. Go back up — it's the missed step, it gets everybody once.
    • OBS: check the source isn't muted in the Audio Mixer, and that "Control audio via OBS" is set how you expect for that source.
  4. Nothing at all? Reload/refresh the browser layer, then re-copy the link from your dashboard — links copied from an old screenshot or a chat log can be stale. The dashboard link is the truth.

More fixes live in Stream Broke? The Big Five Fixes.

Related guides: Alerts misbehaving? Stream Troubleshooting: The Big Five Fixes. Want the whole look in one theme — overlays, panels and alerts that match? See the stream packs page. Free bits to customize with: the Free Resources shelf.

faq.q: Why do my alerts show but make no sound in Meld?
faq.a: A Meld browser layer is silent by default. Select the layer, and in the Inspector under the URL field turn on Add an audio track for the source. Turn on CUE if you want to hear them yourself.

faq.q: What size should my overlay be in OBS?
faq.a: 1920 × 1080 for a full-screen overlay. A standalone alert box is usually 800 × 600 — the toolkit tells you the size on the same screen you copied the link from.

faq.q: Where do I paste an overlay link in OBS?
faq.a: Sources → + → Browser, then paste the link in the URL field. Drag the source to the top of the list so alerts draw over your game, not under it.

guides.title: Stream Audio Setup: How to Make Your Mic Sound Good in Meld and OBS
guides.one_liner: Make your mic sound good: levels, fan and keyboard cleanup, music ducking, and the echo hunt.
guides.description: Stream audio setup in plain steps: pick the right mic, set levels, kill fan and keyboard noise, duck music under your voice, and fix echo — in Meld Studio and OBS.
guides.body:
Real talk: viewers forgive a soft picture. They do NOT forgive bad audio. A buzzing, echoing, whisper-quiet mic ends streams faster than any other problem. The good news — the fixes are simple, and both Meld and OBS have the tools built in.

The four jobs of stream audio

  1. Pick the right mic (the app must listen to the device you think it is)
  2. Set your level (loud enough, never distorting)
  3. Clean the room up (fans, keyboards, echo)
  4. Hear yourself safely (headphones, not speakers — speakers feed the mic and your viewers hear everything twice)

Whichever app you run: normal speaking voice should bounce the meter in the green into yellow. Living in the red means clipping — that crunchy distortion nobody can un-hear.

In Meld Studio ⭐

Add and level your mic

  1. In the Audio Mixer, click + to add a track and choose your microphone.
  2. Talk at stream volume; set the track fader so peaks touch yellow, not red.
  3. Tracks are per-scene aware: a classic setup mutes the mic on "Starting Soon" and "BRB" scenes while it stays live on your main scene. Your voice, your rules.

Kill the fan and the keyboard: Voice Clarity

  1. On your mic track, click the + in the filters rack.
  2. Add Voice Clarity. (Older Meld versions: Magic Mic — same job.)
  3. Pick a strength — start at Moderate. Too high can nibble the ends of your words; too low leaves the fan. Moderate is the honest middle.
  4. Voice Clarity also has automatic gain: it rides your volume for you, so quiet talk stays hearable and a laugh doesn't blow the doors off.

Music ducking: Compression

Want game or music to dip under your voice automatically?

  1. Add the Compression filter to the GAME or MUSIC track (not the mic).
  2. Set your microphone as the sidechain.
  3. Now when you talk, that track dips; when you stop, it fades back. Adjust how fast it fades back until it feels natural.

Hear yourself: CUE

Turn on CUE on a track to monitor it in your headphones. CUE is your ears only — it doesn't change what viewers hear. Keep monitoring in headphones, always.

In OBS Studio

Set the mic

  1. Settings → Audio → Mic/Auxiliary Audio = your microphone.
  2. Sample Rate: 48 kHz. Then open your system sound settings and set the mic's format to 48 kHz there too ("2 channel, 24 bit, 48000 Hz" on Windows). Mismatched rates = slow drift out of sync.

Clean it up with filters

On the mic source in the Audio Mixer (gear icon → Filters):

  • Noise Suppression — pick RNNoise; it eats fan hum and room tone better than the basic option.
  • Noise Gate — cuts the mic entirely when you're not talking. A close threshold around −30 to −25 dB is a sane start.
  • Compressor — evens out quiet talk vs loud reactions.

Monitoring without the echo

In Advanced Audio Properties (mixer gear), monitoring for most sources should be Monitor Off. "Monitor and Output" plays your voice back at you — through speakers, that's an instant echo loop. If you monitor, headphones only, and never monitor a source into the same device you're also capturing as desktop audio.

The two audio gremlins (quick versions)

Echo / your voice twice: something is playing your mic back into itself — speakers on, monitoring set to Monitor-and-Output, the mic added twice (once global, once as a scene source), or your own stream open unmuted in a browser tab. Full hunt in the troubleshooting guide.

Voice drifting out of sync over a long stream: sample-rate mismatch, almost every time. Match everything to 48 kHz. Still off by a fixed amount? In OBS, Advanced Audio Properties → Sync Offset on the mic, adjusted in small steps (50–200 ms is typical), tested with a hand-clap on camera.

One honest gap: as of late 2026, Meld's public docs don't describe a per-track sync-offset dial like OBS has. If your voice drifts in Meld, match your mic to 48 kHz in system settings and re-add the track — and if it still drifts, that's a tell-us case, not a you-problem.

🧰 Field note — from the bench: CleanDEE's mic chain and settings — what he actually runs, fan noise and all — goes here when he writes it.

Related guides: Echo or drift right now? Stream Troubleshooting: The Big Five Fixes. Still setting up? How to Set Up Meld Studio or How to Set Up OBS Studio for Streaming.

faq.q: Why does my stream audio echo?
faq.a: Something is playing your mic back into itself: speakers instead of headphones, monitoring set to Monitor and Output, the mic added twice, or your own stream open unmuted in a browser tab. The full hunt is in the troubleshooting guide.

faq.q: Why does my voice drift out of sync on a long stream?
faq.a: Sample-rate mismatch, almost every time. Set your mic and the app to 48 kHz — in system settings too — and the drift goes away.

faq.q: How do I stop my mic picking up my fan and keyboard?
faq.a: In Meld, add the Voice Clarity filter to your mic track (start at Moderate). In OBS, use Noise Suppression (RNNoise) plus a Noise Gate on the mic source.

faq.q: Should I monitor my own voice?
faq.a: Headphones only, and in OBS leave most sources on Monitor Off — "Monitor and Output" through speakers is an instant echo loop.

guides.title: Why Is My Stream Blurry? The Bitrate Math That Fixes It
guides.one_liner: Stream looks like it was filmed through a shower door? It's bitrate. Here's the math that fixes it.
guides.description: Stream looks blurry or pixelated when you move? It's bitrate. The simple math — upload speed, bitrate, resolution — and the exact settings for Kick and Twitch.
guides.body:
Your game looks crisp on your monitor. Your stream looks like it was filmed through a shower door. Nine times out of ten, that's not your camera or your PC — it's bitrate: how much picture data you send per second.

Think of bitrate as the size of the pipe. A calm talking scene sips data. A fast game — racing, shooters, anything with grass — GULPS it. Same pipe, not enough water: the picture smears. That's the blur.

The only three numbers that matter

  1. Your upload speed. Test it (speedtest.net). Not the number on your internet bill — the number you actually get, right now.
  2. Your bitrate. What you tell the app to send.
  3. Your resolution + frame rate. Bigger picture, more frames = more data needed to stay sharp.

The rules that keep you safe

  • Kick's rule: upload at least TWICE your bitrate. 6,000 kbps stream → 12 Mbps upload or don't.
  • The 70% rule (OBS crowd's version of the same idea): never set bitrate above ~70% of your tested upload. Your internet also has to live its own life.
  • Whichever rule you use: leave headroom. A stream at the ragged edge doesn't look better — it drops frames and looks worse.

What each platform allows

PlatformMax bitrateHard rules
Kick8,000 kbpsH.264 only, CBR only, 2s keyframe, up to 1080p60
Twitch6,000 kbps (non-affiliate guideline)CBR, 2s keyframe
Multistream to both6,000 kbpsThe strictest platform sets the number

Pick your pairing (don't just max the slider)

PictureBitrateUpload you need
1080p, 60 fps6,000–8,000 kbps12–16 Mbps
720p, 60 fps4,000–5,000 kbps10 Mbps
720p, 30 fps3,000–4,500 kbps9 Mbps

Here's the secret nobody tells new streamers: 1080p at a starved bitrate looks WORSE than 720p at a healthy one. If your upload is modest, own 720p and make it clean. Viewers pick smooth and sharp over big and blurry, every time.

Where to set it

Meld ⭐: Settings → General sets your Main Canvas. Your Stream Settings → Resolution is separate — you can stream at 720p while your canvas (and recording) stays 1080p. Turn the hardware encoder ON (NVENC on NVIDIA cards) in your output settings so your graphics card does the heavy lifting, not your CPU.

OBS: Settings → Output (switch to Advanced) for encoder, rate control (CBR), bitrate and the 2-second keyframe interval. Settings → Video for base and output resolution — streaming at 720p = Output (Scaled) Resolution 1280×720.

Use a hardware encoder if you have one: NVENC (NVIDIA), QuickSync (Intel), AMF (AMD). Software encoding (x264) makes your CPU encode video AND run your game. That's how "encoding overloaded" is born.

Still blurry? Work the list

  1. Are you actually sending the bitrate you set? (Dropped frames mean the pipe is failing — see the troubleshooting guide.)
  2. Is your upload shared right now? Someone streaming video in the next room eats your pipe.
  3. Wi-Fi? Plug in an ethernet cable and test again. Wi-Fi lies; cables don't.
  4. Fast-motion game at 1080p60 on 4,500 kbps? That's the blur, mathematically guaranteed. Raise bitrate or drop to 720p60.

🧰 Field note — from the bench: CleanDEE streams FPV drone footage — about the highest-motion video there is. His bitrate lessons from the drone feed go here.

Related guides: Frames dropping as well? Stream Troubleshooting: The Big Five Fixes. First setup? How to Set Up Meld Studio or How to Set Up OBS Studio for Streaming.

faq.q: Why is my stream blurry even though my internet is good?
faq.a: Usually the pairing, not the pipe: 1080p at a starved bitrate looks worse than 720p at a healthy one. Either raise the bitrate (if your upload allows) or drop to 720p and feed it properly.

faq.q: Why does my stream get pixelated when I move in-game?
faq.a: Fast motion gulps data. A calm scene sips; a shooter or racing game at the same bitrate runs dry, and the picture smears into blocks. More bitrate, or less picture — those are the only two levers.

faq.q: What bitrate should I use for 1080p60?
faq.a: 6,000–8,000 kbps, with 12–16 Mbps of real upload behind it. Kick caps at 8,000; Twitch's guideline tops out at 6,000.

faq.q: Is 720p better than 1080p for streaming?
faq.a: On a modest upload, yes — smooth and sharp beats big and blurry, and viewers pick the clean picture every time.

guides.title: Stream Troubleshooting: Dropped Frames, Echo, Black Screen — The Big Five Fixes
guides.one_liner: Dropped frames, echo, black screen, silent alerts — the big five, and the fix for each.
guides.description: Stream keeps lagging, echoing, or showing a black screen? The five problems every streamer hits — dropped frames, echo, out-of-sync voice, black capture, silent alerts — and the fix for each.
guides.body:
Everything breaks live, eventually, in front of everybody. It is not a talent issue — it's a plumbing issue. Here are the five problems every streamer meets, how to tell them apart, and the fix that actually works. Work them in order; don't change five things at once or you'll never know what fixed it.

1. Dropped frames and lag — "my stream is a slideshow"

First job: figure out WHOSE fault it is. There are three different problems wearing the same coat.

In OBS, open View → Stats and read the lines:

  • Dropped Frames (Network) climbing → your INTERNET. The data isn't reaching the platform.
  • Skipped Frames (Encoding Lag) → your CPU is overloaded.
  • Frames Missed (Rendering Lag) → your GPU is overloaded.

In Meld, for a capture that stutters: open View → Open Capture Device Stats. The FPS graphs show if a camera or capture layer is producing fewer frames than it should. Meld's own docs name the usual causes: a faulty connection to an external camera, the camera sitting in low-light mode, a CPU/GPU bottleneck (a heavy game plus an AI camera filter is a classic combo).

Fixes — internet side

  1. Lower your bitrate. No more than ~70% of your tested upload (Kick wants upload at least 2× your bitrate). One notch fixes most cases.
  2. Ethernet cable. Wi-Fi is the silent killer of streams.
  3. Drop the picture before you drop the stream: 720p is a perfectly honorable resolution.

Fixes — computer side

  1. Use the hardware encoder (NVENC / QuickSync / AMF) instead of x264 software encoding.
  2. Lower output resolution (1080p → 720p) and/or encoder preset load.
  3. Close the fifteen browser tabs. You know the ones.

2. Echo — "I can hear myself twice"

Something is playing your voice back into your mic. Hunt these, in order:

  1. Speakers on? Headphones. Always. Speakers feed the mic.
  2. Your own stream open in a browser tab? Mute it or close it.
  3. Mic added twice? In OBS, a mic set globally (Settings → Audio) AND added as a scene source gets captured twice. Delete one. Same trap in Meld: the same device on two tracks.
  4. Monitoring loop? OBS: Advanced Audio Properties — monitoring should be Monitor Off unless you deliberately need it, and never "Monitor and Output" through speakers. Meld: CUE is headphones-only for the same reason.
  5. Windows "Listen to this device" turned on for your mic? Turn it off.

3. Voice out of sync — "your lips lie"

  1. Match sample rates everywhere: 48 kHz. System sound settings for the mic AND playback device, and in OBS Settings → Audio. A 44.1 kHz mic against a 48 kHz stream drifts slowly out of sync over a long stream — this is THE cause.
  2. Fixed offset in OBS: Audio Mixer gear → Advanced Audio Properties → Sync Offset on the mic. Small steps — 50–200 ms is the usual range. Test with a hand-clap on camera in a short recording: adjust until the clap you SEE matches the clap you HEAR.
  3. Meld, honestly: Meld's public docs don't describe a sync offset dial (as of late 2026). Do the 48 kHz match in your system settings, re-add the mic track, and if it still drifts, tell us — that's a case we want to learn from, not hide.

4. Capture shows black / nothing at all

Meld ⭐ — camera won't show:

  1. Check camera permissions: Windows Settings → Privacy & Security → Camera — Camera access ON, "Let apps access your camera" ON, Meld Studio allowed.
  2. Close anything else holding the camera (video call apps grab it first and don't share).
  3. Still nothing? Select the layer and try Use Alternate Capture Backend in the video device settings — it switches stubborn devices to the older DirectShow path.
  4. Camera lagging instead of missing? View → Open Capture Device Stats (see #1) — check the cable, the light, and the load.

OBS — game capture black screen:

  1. Run OBS as administrator. Games at admin level are invisible to a non-admin OBS. This one fix solves a huge share of cases.
  2. Switch the capture type. Game Capture for fullscreen games, Window Capture for apps, Display Capture for the whole desktop. Wrong type = black box.
  3. Laptop with two GPUs? OBS and the game must run on the SAME graphics card — set both in Windows graphics settings.
  4. Turn off other overlays (Discord, Steam, GeForce) — they can hijack the layer OBS is trying to read.
  5. Some games' anti-cheat blocks capture by design, and streaming services (Netflix etc.) are black on purpose. That's not broken — that's locked.

5. Alerts show but stay silent — or never show at all

  1. Send a TEST alert first (from your toolkit dashboard, or your alert provider's). Never debug against real followers.
  2. Is the layer even awake? OBS: the source's eye icon is on and the source sits ABOVE your game in the list. Meld: the Browser layer isn't hidden in the Layers panel.
  3. Silent alerts in Meld: browser layers make NO sound until you turn on Add an audio track for the source under the URL field (Inspector). This is the most-missed step in Meld, full stop.
  4. Refresh the source. OBS: right-click the Browser source → Properties → Refresh. Meld: the reload icon next to the URL.
  5. Stale link? If you reset a token or regenerated a widget anywhere, every old browser source pointing at the old URL is dead. Re-copy the link from the dashboard. (Your ForeverHumans overlay link never changes — one more reason it's built that way.)
  6. Picture frozen but sound plays (OBS): toggle Settings → Advanced → Browser Source Hardware Acceleration and restart OBS. Either direction can be the fix — whatever it is now, flip it.
  7. Last resort: delete the source and re-add it fresh with a freshly copied link. Corrupted scene configs die hard.

Fixed it with something not on this list? That's gold. Field notes from real streamers get added to these guides with your handle on them — send them through the toolkit feedback box.

faq.q: How do I fix dropped frames?
faq.a: In OBS, open View → Stats: network drops mean internet (lower your bitrate to ~70% of your tested upload, plug in ethernet); encoding lag means switch to the hardware encoder; rendering lag means your GPU needs room. One fix at a time, then retest.

faq.q: Why does my stream echo?
faq.a: Your voice is playing back into your mic — speakers on, your own stream open in a tab, the mic added twice, or monitoring set to Monitor and Output. Fix #2 above walks the hunt in order.

faq.q: Why is my game capture black in OBS?
faq.a: Run OBS as administrator first — that one fix solves a huge share of cases. Then check the capture type matches the game, and that OBS and the game are on the same graphics card.

faq.q: Why are my alerts silent?
faq.a: In Meld, browser layers make no sound until you turn on Add an audio track for the source. In OBS, check the source isn't muted in the Audio Mixer. Always debug with a test alert, never against real followers.
